item.title: Gitea CVE-2026-20896 exploitation, Injective npm compromise, and ShareFile shutdown warning
item.content:encoded:
Hackers exploit critical auth bypass in Gitea Docker image — Must Read

Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20896, a critical authentication bypass in default Gitea Docker images that lets unauthenticated attackers impersonate any user, including admins, by spoofing a trusted reverse-proxy header. Gitea users should upgrade to version 1.26.4 or restrict REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to trusted IPs and review logs for compromise.

  • Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20896, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in the official Docker image for the Gitea self-hosted Git service.
  • The flaw affects official Gitea Docker images up to and including version 1.26.2 in the default configuration, where reverse proxy authentication headers such as X-WEBAUTH-USER are enabled.
  • The default setting REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=* causes Gitea to trust the X-WEBAUTH-USER header from any source IP, allowing unauthenticated attackers to impersonate arbitrary users, including administrators.
  • Gitea released versions 1.26.3 and 1.26.4 to address CVE-2026-20896 and advised users to upgrade directly to the most recent release.
  • Singapore’s cybersecurity agency warned that CVE-2026-20896 is being actively exploited and recommended restricting REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES to specific trusted IP addresses if upgrading is not possible.

Progress urges ShareFile admins to shut down servers over “credible” threat — Must Read

Progress Software is telling ShareFile customers using on-premises Storage Zone Controllers to immediately shut down those servers due to a credible external security threat. The company says it has temporarily disabled affected ShareFile access and has not yet confirmed any unauthorized access or data compromise.

  • Progress Software emailed ShareFile customers using Storage Zone Controllers and urged them to immediately shut down their servers due to a “credible external security threat.”
  • Progress said it has no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile accounts or data, but it temporarily disabled access to ShareFile accounts using Storage Zone Controllers as a precaution.
  • Progress instructed customers to manually shut down the Windows servers hosting Storage Zone Controllers, stating that this is a critical additional step to ensure data safety.
  • The ShareFile status page states that ShareFile customers with Storage Zone Controllers are not operational at this time.
  • Progress has not disclosed whether the threat involves a zero-day vulnerability or whether any Storage Zone Controllers have been compromised.

Injective Labs GitHub Compromise Pushes Wallet-Key-Stealing npm Packages — Should Read

Attackers compromised Injective Labs’ GitHub/npm release process to publish malicious @injectivelabs packages that stole crypto wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when used. Anyone who installed the affected 1.20.21 packages should upgrade to a clean version and treat any keys or seed phrases processed by them as compromised.

  • Unknown threat actors compromised the Injective Labs SDK project's GitHub repository and used it to publish the malicious npm package @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21.
  • The malicious version contained fake telemetry functionality that exfiltrated cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases when affected library functionality was used.
  • The threat actor also published version 1.20.21 across 17 additional @injectivelabs scoped packages that depended on and pinned the malicious SDK version, affecting potential transitive users.
  • The exfiltration mechanism queued multiple key derivations over a two-second window and sent them in an HTTPS POST request to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective[.]network.
  • Users who installed the malicious version are advised to update to the clean version 1.20.23, treat any private key or mnemonic phrase passed through the package as compromised, rotate them, and check for transitive dependencies.

Police suspects Dutch hackers were involved in Odido breach — Should Read

Dutch police say they have strong indications that Dutch hackers were involved in Odido’s February data breach, including a vishing call in which a Dutch-speaking man impersonated an IT employee before phishing led to data theft. The breach exposed personal data of millions of customers and was claimed by the ShinyHunters extortion gang.

  • The Dutch National Police said it found strong indications that Dutch hackers were involved in a February breach at telecommunications provider Odido.
  • Police said a Dutch-speaking man posed as an Odido IT employee during a call with customer service shortly before the hack, after which the company was misled through phishing and data theft occurred.
  • Odido disclosed on February 12 that attackers accessed its customer contact system on February 7 and downloaded personal data affecting 6.2 million customers.
  • The exposed information may include names, addresses, cities of residence, mobile numbers, customer numbers, email addresses, IBANs, dates of birth, and some passport or driver’s license details, but not call details, location data, billing data, identity document scans, or Mijn Odido passwords.
  • The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility for the breach and released an 88GB archive containing over 15 million records on its dark web leak site.

Six New U-Boot Flaws Could Let Malicious Images Crash Devices or Run Code at Boot — Should Read

Binarly found six U-Boot flaws in FIT image signature verification, including two that could allow code execution before a device verifies boot software. Vendors using U-Boot should pull the upstream patches now because no fixed stable release is available yet.

  • Binarly found six flaws in U-Boot, a bootloader used in devices such as home routers, smart cameras, and server management chips.
  • The flaws affect U-Boot’s handling of FIT images during signature verification and are reachable while U-Boot is still reading an untrusted image before checking the signature.
  • Two flaws, BRLY-2026-037 and BRLY-2026-038, could allow attacker-supplied code to run at boot because U-Boot uses unchecked values returned by fdt_get_name.
  • Four flaws, BRLY-2026-039, BRLY-2026-040, BRLY-2026-041, and BRLY-2026-042, can crash the bootloader through out-of-bounds reads, a null pointer dereference, or stack exhaustion.
  • U-Boot merged patches for the six flaws in June, but there is no stable release containing the fixes yet, so vendors and maintainers are advised to pull the upstream fixes now.

Researcher Details WhatsApp-to-Host Attack Chain Using Three OpenClaw Flaws — Should Read

Three now-patched OpenClaw flaws could let attackers trigger credential theft, privilege escalation, sandbox escape, and host code execution, reportedly even from an external WhatsApp message. Users should upgrade to OpenClaw 2026.6.6 and restrict risky tool access such as exec for untrusted or channel-facing agents.

  • Three now-patched high-severity flaws in the OpenClaw personal AI assistant could enable credential theft, privilege escalation, and arbitrary code execution on the host.
  • The vulnerabilities are tracked as GHSA-hjr6-g723-hmfm, GHSA-9969-8g9h-rxwm, and GHSA-575v-8hfq-m3mc, and all three were fixed in OpenClaw version 2026.6.6.
  • Security researcher Chinmohan Nayak said the flaws can be used to trigger host code execution from an external message sent via WhatsApp.
  • GHSA-575v-8hfq-m3mc involves a path traversal and link following issue that could allow sandbox bind mounts to bypass parent-directory denylist checks.
  • The article recommends upgrading OpenClaw, enabling sandbox mode for all non-main sessions, removing exec from the tool allowlist for channel-facing agents, and monitoring for git clone commands using the ext:: external protocol helper.

Ryuk ransomware member pleads guilty in the US, faces 15 years in prison — Should Read

Karen Serobovich Vardanyan, an Armenian Ryuk ransomware operator extradited to the U.S., pleaded guilty to helping hack and encrypt U.S. organizations’ networks between 2019 and 2020. He faces up to 15 years in prison and agreed to pay more than $1.1 million in restitution.

  • Karen Serobovich Vardanyan, a 34-year-old Armenian man, pleaded guilty in the United States to hacking U.S. companies and deploying Ryuk ransomware to encrypt their systems.
  • Vardanyan was extradited to the United States after being arrested in Kyiv in April 2025 for providing initial access to corporate networks.
  • According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Vardanyan and his co-conspirators received about 1,610 bitcoins in ransom payments, valued at around $15 million at the time.
  • The Ryuk ransomware operation was active from 2018 until mid-2020 and targeted organizations across nearly every sector, including healthcare providers during the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • Vardanyan is scheduled to be sentenced in September 2026 and faces a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison, fines of $250,000 for each charge, and more than $1.1 million in restitution.

Laser Attack Resets Tangem Wallet Passwords on Cards That Can't Be Patched — May Read

Ledger Donjon researchers showed that a costly, invasive laser fault-injection attack can reset passwords on Tangem wallet cards without the old password or backup card, potentially letting someone with physical possession move funds. The risk is low for most users because it requires a specialized lab and visibly destroys the card, but lost or stolen cards holding significant value should be treated as unsafe.

  • Ledger's Donjon security team demonstrated that a precisely timed laser pulse aimed at the chip inside a Tangem crypto wallet card can reset the card's password to an attacker-chosen value.
  • The attack requires physical possession of the card, cutting it open to expose the chip, specialized equipment estimated at about $250,000, and cannot be performed over the internet.
  • Tangem cards cannot receive firmware updates, so cards already sold cannot be patched against this flaw.
  • Tangem said the method is a lab-only physical attack, noted that Donjon belongs to rival Ledger, and argued that the practical risk for everyday users is virtually non-existent.
  • The article advises users whose Tangem card is lost or stolen and holds serious value to move their funds using another card in the set or a seed phrase if available.

License plate cameras may be next target after Supreme Court reins in location tracking — May Read

A recent Supreme Court ruling requiring warrants for cell phone geofence location searches could strengthen legal challenges to warrantless automated license plate reader searches. Experts say the decision may force courts to scrutinize ALPR networks as broad, retrospective surveillance systems, while Flock Safety argues its cameras are legally distinct because they capture vehicles in public view.

  • The Supreme Court’s Chatrie v. United States ruling found that searches of cell phone location history require a warrant and addressed law enforcement use of private location data.
  • Legal scholars and opponents of automated license plate readers say the Chatrie ruling could affect how police use ALPR databases because such systems collect retrospective and indiscriminate location information.
  • Flock Safety says it has between 90,000 and 100,000 cameras installed on public roadways and collects data on about 20 billion license plates per month.
  • Flock Safety said the Supreme Court decision is not relevant to its technology because ALPR captures point-in-time images of vehicles in public view, unlike Google location history from mobile devices.
  • Andrew Guthrie Ferguson said modern ALPR systems connect to larger police and public databases that can include social media activity, surveillance video, body camera footage, drone footage, gunshot sensor data, and dashboard camera footage.

Money launderer accused of stealing seized crypto while in prison — May Read

Bulgarian national Rossen Iossifov, already imprisoned for laundering funds from online auction fraud victims, has been charged with stealing $290,000 in government-seized cryptocurrency from behind bars. Prosecutors say he routed the funds through exchanges and mixing services to evade forfeiture, and he faces up to 25 more years if convicted.

  • Bulgarian national Rossen G. Iossifov has been charged with stealing $290,000 in government-seized cryptocurrency while serving a 121-month prison sentence.
  • Prosecutors allege that in January 2024, Iossifov conspired with others to move the cryptocurrency from a seized account through multiple crypto exchanges and mixing services.
  • Iossifov’s earlier conviction was tied to his operation of RG Coins, a cryptocurrency exchange in Sofia, Bulgaria, used by Romanian members of the Alexandria Online Auction Fraud Network.
  • The Alexandria Online Auction Fraud Network posted fake Craigslist and eBay ads for high-value goods, often vehicles, and victimized at least 900 Americans.
  • If convicted on the new charges of removal of property to prevent seizure and conspiracy to commit money laundering, Iossifov faces up to 25 years in prison.

The Replicant in Your Directory: AI Agents and the Identity Security Gap — Optional

AI agents and other machine identities are rapidly expanding enterprise identity footprints faster than traditional governance can manage, creating trusted access paths that attackers can abuse. Organizations need continuous ownership, access, and lifecycle controls for non-human identities, not just visibility.

  • The article argues that identity security programs were originally built around human lifecycle events, while AI agents, service accounts, OAuth applications, workload identities, and other machine identities often do not follow those patterns.
  • The Non-Human Identity Management Group says machine identities now outnumber human users by as much as 50 to one in many environments.
  • In 2025, the threat actor UNC6395 obtained an OAuth token associated with Salesloft's Drift chat integration and used it to move through Salesforce environments across hundreds of organizations.
  • Netwrix reported that organizations where AI significantly expanded the number of identities had a 43% breach rate over the previous year, compared with 11% among organizations where AI had not significantly changed their identity footprint.
  • The article says security teams need continuous answers about what identities exist, who owns them, what they can access, and when they should no longer exist.
